text: The number of one-one functions that can be defined from a set $A$ containing $3$ elements into a set $B$ containing $5$ elements is:

solution.keyConcept: A one-one (injective) function must send the 3 distinct elements of $A$ to 3 distinct images in $B$: an ordered selection of 3 out of 5, i.e. the arrangement ${}^{5}P_{3}$.
formulas: \text{injections from } A \text{ (} m \text{ elements) to } B \text{ (} n \text{ elements)} = {}^{n}P_{m} = \dfrac{n!}{(n-m)!}
solution.body:
**Step 1 — Fix the images one element at a time.**
The first element of $A$ has $5$ possible images; the second must avoid the first image ($4$ left); the third must avoid both ($3$ left).

**Step 2 — Multiply (multiplication principle).**
$$5 \times 4 \times 3 = 60$$
solution.commonMistakes: Answering $\binom{5}{3} = 10$ — that counts the sets of images, ignoring which element maps where. Answering $5^3 = 125$ — that allows repeated images, i.e. all functions, not injective ones.
solution.verification: Formula check: ${}^{5}P_{3} = \dfrac{5!}{2!} = \dfrac{120}{2} = 60$, and the total count of all functions $5^3 = 125$ correctly exceeds it. ✓

text: Which of the following statements are true?
options: The contrapositive of the statement $p \rightarrow q$ is $\sim q \rightarrow \sim p$
The disjunction $p \lor q$ is true only when both $p$ and $q$ are true
'$\sqrt{2}$ is an irrational number' is a statement (proposition) in logic
The negation of a true statement is always a true statement

solution.keyConcept: The contrapositive of $p \rightarrow q$ is $\sim q \rightarrow \sim p$ (logically equivalent to the original). A disjunction is true when at least one component is true. A proposition is a declarative sentence with a definite truth value. Negation flips the truth value.
formulas: p \rightarrow q \equiv \sim q \rightarrow \sim p, \qquad p \lor q \text{ is true iff at least one of } p, q \text{ is true}
solution.body:
**Step 1 — Option A (contrapositive).**
By definition the contrapositive of $p \rightarrow q$ is $\sim q \rightarrow \sim p$. ✔ True.

**Step 2 — Option B (disjunction).**
$F \lor T$ is true with only one component true — 'only when both are true' describes the conjunction $p \land q$, not the disjunction. ✘ False.

**Step 3 — Option C (proposition).**
'$\sqrt{2}$ is irrational' is a declarative sentence with a definite truth value (true), so it is a proposition. ✔ True.

**Step 4 — Option D (negation).**
The negation of a true statement is false, not true. ✘ False.
solution.commonMistakes: Confusing the contrapositive with the converse ($q \rightarrow p$). Reading 'only when both' as 'when both' — the word only makes option B the definition of conjunction.
solution.verification: Truth-table check of A: the columns of $p \rightarrow q$ and $\sim q \rightarrow \sim p$ agree on all four rows. For B, the row $p = F, q = T$ gives $F \lor T = T$ — a direct counterexample to 'only when both'. ✓

text: One card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled standard deck of $52$ cards. The probability that the card drawn is either a spade or an ace is:

solution.keyConcept: Use the addition rule with inclusion-exclusion: $P(S \cup A) = P(S) + P(A) - P(S \cap A)$. The ace of spades lies in both events and must not be counted twice.
formulas: P(S \cup A) = P(S) + P(A) - P(S \cap A)
solution.body:
**Step 1 — Count the events.**
Spades: $13$ cards. Aces: $4$ cards. Ace of spades: $1$ card (counted in both).

**Step 2 — Inclusion-exclusion.**
$$|S \cup A| = 13 + 4 - 1 = 16$$

**Step 3 — Probability.**
$$P(S \cup A) = \frac{16}{52} = \frac{4}{13}$$
solution.commonMistakes: Adding to $13 + 4 = 17$ (giving $17/52$) — the ace of spades gets counted twice. Counting the ace of spades as four aces inside the spades.
solution.verification: Direct recount: $12$ non-ace spades $+$ ace of spades $+$ $3$ other aces $= 16$ favourable cards, and $16/52 = 4/13$. ✓

subtopic: Magnitude of the sum of orthogonal vectors

solution.keyConcept: The squared magnitude of a sum expands with the dot product: $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}|^2 = |\vec{a}|^2 + |\vec{b}|^2 + 2\,\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}$. Orthogonality kills the cross term, leaving Pythagoras.
solution.body:
**Step 1 — Expand the squared magnitude.**
With $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 0$:
$$|\vec{a}+\vec{b}|^2 = 3^2 + 4^2 + 0 = 25$$

**Step 2 — Take the positive square root.**
$$|\vec{a}+\vec{b}| = 5$$
solution.commonMistakes: Adding the magnitudes directly ($3 + 4 = 7$) — valid only for parallel vectors. Forgetting the square root and answering $25$.
solution.verification: Concrete instance: $\vec{a} = 3\hat{i}$ and $\vec{b} = 4\hat{j}$ give $\vec{a}+\vec{b} = 3\hat{i}+4\hat{j}$ with magnitude $\sqrt{9+16} = 5$ — the classic 3-4-5 triple. ✓
